title: FastCREST: GPU-Accelerated CREST Conformer Searches with Consistent Energies and Gradients
summary: CREST conformer searches with GFN2-xTB take days for large, flexible molecules: one search of a 274-atom gallium(III)--peptide complex with CREST 3.0.2 took 321.5~h on 32 CPU threads. FastCREST keeps CREST's algorithm and changes how a search uses the hardware. Its metadynamics (MTD) and molecular dynamics (MD) trajectories run with tuned OpenMP settings and one GPU, which solves the self-consistent-charge (SCC) eigenproblem and evaluates the three-body dispersion term. About 15,000 geometry optimizations per iteration run as Slurm array jobs on other CPU nodes, and checkpoints let a search continue on preemptible GPUs. On A100 nodes, the OpenMP settings and loop changes made an MTD step 2.4 times faster and the GPU another 2.3 times; array jobs made a batch of optimizations 39 times faster. For six more molecules of 24 to 339 atoms, a FastCREST step was 2.2 to 7.1 times faster than a conventional CREST step. A complete FastCREST search, which also lifts CREST~3's cap of 200 optimization cycles, took 54.3~h, evaluating energies and gradients 8.1 times as fast as the CREST 3.0.2 search (on different hardware) with fewer CPU-hours per evaluation. Two opt-in settings (a warm-started Jacobi eigensolver and GPU-resident SCC iterations), LLVM's OpenMP library and one CPU socket per trajectory made an MTD step 8.3 times faster than conventional CREST. Energies agree with CREST 3.0.2 within $1.01\times10^{-10}$ Eh and gradients within $8.2\times10^{-11}$Eh bohr$^{-1}$, and controlled MD runs passed a prespecified equivalence test. Most replicate FastCREST and conventional CREST searches ended in similar compact conformers, with no detectable difference in energy.

title: General-purpose language models are neurosymbolic reasoners able to annotate proteins from sequence
summary:
Determining the function of genes across the tree of life is one of the major challenges in biology. Generative AI approaches to this problem generally fall into two categories: language models trained on biological sequences that are able to predict structure and function from signals in those sequences; and generalist language models trained on text, that are able to reason about biological function symbolically. A default operating assumption is that protein language models do not perform well on symbolic tasks, and that generalist language models do not perform well on sequence tasks. However, a recent report showed that frontier generalist models perform surprisingly well on next-residue prediction tasks. We set out to explore whether these capabilities extended to protein annotation.
  We assigned different frontier generalist models a variety of protein annotation tasks, including predicting the presence and coordinates of Pfam domains, loss of functional catalytic residues, and predicting structure and activity. On all annotation tasks, the frontier models performed well above chance; we did not benchmark them against specialised tools. The models also make characteristic hallucination errors, and they state them as confidently as their correct calls.
  Though untested against specialised methods, the nascent ability of frontier models to perform protein annotation from sequence alone is intriguing. The ability to reason over sequence, structure, and symbols in a single model allows for a neurosymbolic approach where a combination of sequence, experimental data and knowledge from the literature can be holistically combined to improve on de novo functional annotation of the protein universe.
  Prompts, test sets, model outputs and code: https://github.com/ai4curation/fable-sequence-to-function. Summary of results: https://ai4curation.io/fable-sequence-to-function/

title: RumiFold: Teaching an LLM to Natively Fold Proteins and Reason About Their Function
summary: Can we teach a general-purpose language model to fold proteins? And if so, what does learning to fold enable beyond structure prediction itself? We introduce RumiFold, a pretrained chat model that learns to predict protein structures directly from its own hidden states. RumiFold processes proteins through repeated folding passes, then uses these folded representations to answer questions in natural language. It achieves folding accuracy comparable to dedicated single-representation models such as SimpleFold, alongside state-of-the-art performance on Gene Ontology protein function prediction and free-text function description. We find that folding pretraining organizes the model's hidden states around protein function, creating an internal per-residue workspace that is biologically grounded. Causal interventions show that this folded workspace links structure and language when RumiFold predicts function, providing rich representations for biomolecular reasoning. We see RumiFold as a step toward native biomolecular intelligence: where protein-based computations and language-based reasoning become integrated capabilities of general-purpose language models. Code, data, and models are available at: https://rumifold.baulab.info

title: What Do Co-Folding Models Learn? Insights from Enhanced Transition Path Sampling
summary: Co-folding models are diffusion-based generative models that sample biomolecular complexes from distributions learned on a large corpus of experimental data. Although these models are powerful for structure prediction, it remains unclear whether the conformational ensembles they learn resemble physically meaningful statistical ensembles. To understand what these models learn, we introduce transition path sampling (TPS), which uses Markov chain Monte Carlo over denoising trajectories to sample the learned distribution. Because its Monte Carlo trajectories resemble biomolecular dynamics, TPS couples directly with enhanced-sampling techniques to recover the full conformational ensemble. Applied to Boltz-2, enhanced TPS reveals physical conformational changes biased toward crystal-like states near the training data, indicating both learned physics and memorization. These results suggest new ways to evaluate and improve co-folding models by jointly assessing structural recovery, proximity to training data, and conformational ensembles.

title: Impact of Topology and Sequence Length on the Pressure-Dependent Collapsibility of Proteins
summary: Several physical and evolutionary factors, including temperature, pressure, solvent quality, and natural selection, influence how amino acid sequences adopt their native structures. Although protein folding has been extensively studied, the physical determinants of protein collapse and their relationship to native-state folding remain less understood. In particular, "collapsibility", the intrinsic propensity of a protein sequence to form compact conformations, is distinct from but closely related to "foldability", the ability to reach the native structure. Previous theoretical studies suggested that collapsibility is encoded in native-state topology, potentially reflecting evolutionary selection. However, the roles of solvent-mediated interactions and hydrostatic pressure remain unclear. Here, we extend the theoretical framework of protein collapsibility by incorporating a pressure-dependent desolvation potential to investigate how hydrostatic pressure influences protein collapse. We find that increasing pressure destabilizes the fully folded native state, but can still favor the compact, water-mediated conformations. Furthermore, the magnitude and direction of pressure-induced changes in collapsibility depend strongly on native-state topology, including secondary and tertiary structures. Proteins and domains with a higher proportion of non-local native contacts generally exhibit greater pressure-induced water-mediated collapsibility. These findings highlight the role of native-state topology in determining the pressure sensitivity of protein collapse and provide insights into the interplay among protein structure, solvent-mediated interactions, and environmental perturbations.
